what: An admin log that names who changed what, a curator role that holds knowledge without holding governance, and the closing of a hole this work found on its way there.

the_hole.found: Driving the new attribution end to end meant signing in as somebody who was not an admin, to see what the log recorded. It recorded nothing, because the request succeeded: a signed-in employee in no groups sent DELETE /documents/handbook.md and got 200, the file gone from disk and the corpus one document smaller. `require_uploads` gates on the upload switch, not on who is asking, so readable meant deletable for everyone in the company.
the_hole.the_second_route: The same hole wearing an upload's clothes: POST /documents over an existing filename replaced its contents. A delete and an add, and nothing checked either.
the_hole.fixed: With sign-in on, removing a document - or uploading over one that exists - now needs the curator or admin role, and the refusal says so. Contributing a NEW document still needs only the uploads switch, because contribution is what that switch is for. With sign-in off nothing changed: there is no identity to check, reaching the port was always full control, and a role check against an identity that does not exist would be theatre.

attribution.what_was_missing: folder_access recorded folder, principals and updated_at - what changed, never who. Nothing anywhere recorded who deleted a document, approved a draft, resolved a contradiction or changed a setting. 'Somebody walled off the HR folder last Tuesday' had no answer.
attribution.now: Thirteen mutating admin actions write to an admin_actions table in knowledge.db: at, actor id, actor name, actor kind, action, target, detail. A signed-in person is named by their directory subject id, so the row survives a rename and points at an account somebody can disable.
attribution.what_it_will_not_pretend: A change made with the shared admin token is recorded as 'shared admin token' and names nobody. No amount of logging recovers an identity a shared secret never carried. The endpoint returns `attributed` alongside the entries, the /manage panel and the CLI both say how many name nobody, and with sign-in off they say what would fix it.
attribution.secrets: A settings change records WHICH settings changed and never what they became: an editable value can be a base URL with a password in it, and this table travels in every backup. Pinned by planting a credential in embedding_base_url and asserting it appears nowhere in the log.
attribution.append_only: Nothing in the API deletes from the log, so an admin cannot quietly undo their own change through the app. That is a property of the surface, not of the file - anyone with the server's disk can edit the table like any other - and the docs say exactly that rather than overclaiming.
attribution.the_asymmetry_kept: Admin actions are attributed; questions are not. The gaps report still cannot name anyone who asked (test_the_report_cannot_name_anyone), and the ledger still has no column for it. Who governs is recorded; who is curious is not.

roles.split: OK_OIDC_CURATOR_GROUP. Curators pin answers, approve drafts, resolve contradictions, re-index, run learn, read costs and gaps, and delete or replace documents. Admins additionally change who may read a folder, change settings, apply updates and read the admin log.
roles.why: The people who know the answers are rarely the people who should hold the access rules.
roles.compatible: Every admin is a curator, and an install that never sets a curator group behaves exactly as it did - require_curator with no group configured IS require_admin. Pinned.
roles.refusals_name_the_reason: A signed-in non-admin used to get 401 'invalid admin token', which sent people hunting for a credential that was never theirs. Now: 403 'this account is not an administrator; admin access is granted by the admin group'.

measured.the_matrix: Driven through real HTTP against the fake IdP, three people on one server: admin / curator / employee. Admin: yes to all seven checks. Curator: 403 on the admin log, access rules and settings; yes to pinning, re-indexing, the review queue and deleting a document. Employee: refused all seven.
measured.the_log_reads_back: After the drive: 'Cara Nadeau [person] document.delete old.md', 'Alice Moreau [person] access.set hr'. Names, not roles guessed from actions.
measured.restore_records_itself: A restore is the largest change anyone can make to a company's knowledge in one command, and would otherwise leave no trace. It is written into the restored database after the move, so it survives: 'the server console  restore  carry.zip'. Verified by carrying an install between two data directories on the CLI.
measured.the_browser: /manage checked in Chromium for both roles. Admin sees the settings table and a loaded Admin log panel; curator sees 'Curators do not manage this - an administrator does.' in all three governance panels, and no page errors either time. The test was confirmed to FAIL when the selector it depends on is renamed - a browser test that passes against a broken page proves nothing.

gate: No retrieval, prompt, chunking or grounding change: a new table, a role dependency, thirteen log-writing lines, a UI panel and docs. The cache key policy string is untouched. The golden sets gate answers, and no answer moved, so they were not run.
pinned_by: tests/test_admin_log.py (44 tests), one added to tests/test_backup.py, one added to tests/test_auth_browser.py. 1,057 tests pass.
still_open: The shared admin token remains one secret for all admins - the log records that honestly rather than fixing it. Per-role tokens would need a token table, and the answer for a company is sign-in, not more tokens.

found_on_the_way.what: The chat page never said which build it was, and the update chip never appeared - on a fresh load. `refreshUpdateChip()` and the fetch that fills the version label had drifted inside removeDocument's try block, still at column zero but inside the function, so they ran only after somebody deleted a document.
found_on_the_way.why_it_matters: This is the SECOND independent cause of the original field report, 'I still don't see the update button after several releases'. The first was Inno leaving stale .dist-info directories so installs never received a new version at all; that one was fixed and released. Even on a correctly updated install, the chip still would not have rendered. Two causes, one symptom, and fixing either alone would have left the user's complaint standing.
found_on_the_way.measured: In Chromium, before the fix: #build-version = '' and #update-chip = '' on load; after deleting a document, 'OpenKnowledge v0.4.0'. After the fix: 'OpenKnowledge v0.4.0' and 'Running v0.4.0 - up to date. Check for updates' on load, no interaction.
found_on_the_way.the_guard_that_first_proved_nothing: The browserless CI guard is the one that matters, because CI installs no browser. The first version asserted the boot call appears at column zero in the source - and PASSED against the reintroduced bug, because the spliced lines were at column zero while inside the function. Scope was what was wrong, so the guard now computes brace nesting depth (over source with strings and comments blanked) and asserts an occurrence runs at depth zero. Confirmed to fail when the bug is put back. Third time in this project a green result proved nothing; first time it was caught in the guard before shipping.
